summary: Defines the Expect-CT HTTP header, which lets a site tell browsers to expect valid Signed Certificate Timestamps from Certificate Transparency on connections to it. It helps site operators find misconfigurations in their CT deployment and ensures a misissued certificate would be discoverable in the logs. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A website tells your browser to check that its ID card was written in the public book, and to complain if not.

questions: how to enforce certificate transparency in browsers
how to use expect-ct for monitoring
subtitle: HTTP header for Certificate Transparency compliance monitoring

tldr.problem: Websites need a way to ensure that the certificates they deploy are logged in Certificate Transparency logs. They also want to discover if their certificates are misconfigured with respect to CT requirements.
tldr.mechanism: The Expect-CT header tells browsers to expect valid Signed Certificate Timestamps from Certificate Transparency on connections to that host, and to report failures back to the site.
tldr.outcome: Site operators can detect misconfigurations in their CT deployment and ensure that any misissued certificates would be discoverable in public logs. It is experimental.

today: RFC 9163 is an Experimental specification for the Expect-CT header. It is not part of the HTTP standards track but is being evaluated for deployment to help site operators monitor Certificate Transparency compliance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Expect-CT is an HTTP response header that lets a website declare that it is deploying Signed Certificate Timestamps (SCTs) from Certificate Transparency logs. It is similar to HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) and HPKP (HTTP Public Key Pinning), but focuses specifically on CT compliance.

The header works on a trust-on-first-use (TOFU) basis. The first time a browser visits a site, it records that the site uses Expect-CT. From then on, the browser checks that any certificate served by that site includes valid SCTs. If the browser finds a connection that violates this expectation, it can either report it (report-only mode) or block the connection (enforce mode).

This helps site operators discover misconfigurations in their CT deployment and ensures that if a certificate is misissued, it will be discoverable in the public Certificate Transparency logs.
sections.eli5: Your browser learns that a website cares about CT, so it starts checking that the website's certificate is in the public book every time you visit. If you see something that is not in the public book, the browser tells the website about it.

sections.title: The Expect-CT Header Syntax
sections.content:
The Expect-CT header contains directives that configure how the browser should handle CT compliance. The main directives are:

max-age (required): Specifies how long (in seconds) the browser should remember that this is an Expect-CT host. For example, max-age=86400 means one day.

enforce (optional): If present, tells the browser to block connections that do not comply with CT policy. Without it, the browser only reports violations.

report-uri (optional): A URL where the browser should send reports of CT failures. Must use HTTPS. Example: report-uri="https://example.com/ct-report".

A simple example header looks like: Expect-CT: max-age=86400, enforce. A server can also split directives across multiple header instances.
sections.eli5: The header tells your browser three things: how long to remember this rule, whether to really block bad certificates or just warn about them, and where to send a complaint if something looks wrong.

sections.title: How Browsers Use It
sections.content:
When a browser receives an Expect-CT header over a secure HTTPS connection, it checks that the connection complies with its CT policy. If the connection has valid SCTs (Signed Certificate Timestamps), the browser notes the host as a known Expect-CT host and stores the directives.

Later, when the browser connects to that same host, it applies its CT policy check. If the connection violates the policy (for example, if a certificate does not have SCTs), the browser can either refuse the connection (if enforce is set) or silently report the failure (if only report-uri is set).

The browser MUST ignore Expect-CT headers received over plain HTTP (not HTTPS), and it MUST ignore headers on unknown or expired entries. Browsers MAY set an upper limit on max-age, such as 60 days, to protect against hostile header attacks.
sections.eli5: The browser learns the rule and adds it to a list. Next time you visit, it checks. If something is wrong and the rule says to block (enforce), your browser refuses to connect. If the rule says to report, the browser quietly tells the website what went wrong.

sections.title: Reporting and Failure Handling
sections.content:
When a browser detects that a known Expect-CT host violates the CT policy, it MAY generate a violation report and POST it to the report-uri. The report is a JSON object containing the hostname, the port, the certificate chain, the SCTs that were provided, their validation status, and other details.

If the enforce directive is set, the browser also treats the violation as a connection error and may refuse to load the page (with possible user override). If enforce is not set, the browser only reports the problem.

Site operators can use these reports to discover misconfigurations before they cause real connection failures. For example, if they have deployed a certificate that is not logged in CT, the reports will alert them to the problem.
sections.eli5: If something goes wrong, the browser can send a detailed message back to the website saying 'I found a certificate that was not in the public book.' The website uses this feedback to fix the problem before it breaks things for all users.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
Expect-CT must be deployed carefully. If a site operator sets Expect-CT with enforce and a long max-age, but then makes a mistake in their CT configuration, the browser will refuse connections to that site for weeks, causing a denial of service.

Site operators should deploy Expect-CT with precautions: start with report-only mode (no enforce directive), use reports to verify that everything is working, and gradually increase the max-age as confidence grows. TOFU attacks are also possible: a malicious server could temporarily serve a valid certificate and set a long max-age, then revert to a non-CT-compliant certificate, causing future failures.

The spec recommends an upper limit on max-age of around 30 days. UAs should limit report rates to prevent DOS attacks through flooding of the report-uri endpoint.
sections.eli5: This is a powerful tool but it can break things if you use it wrong. Start cautiously: first report-only mode, then enforce it once you know it works. Be careful not to set it for too long, or one mistake will lock you out.
